archetype.name: Bell Cow (three-down)
archetype.definition: Atlanta's every-down back who takes two-thirds of the team's carries, every goal-line touch and, in a normal year, a top-tier target load, so the offense runs through him whoever is at quarterback.

report.headline: A bell cow carrying a broken offense, with one game inflating the efficiency
report.take:
Robinson is in his fourth season and has been the same player each year: a high-snap, high-touch back who catches the ball as much as anyone at the position, and whose rushing over expected has risen every season, from 0.39 to 0.68 to 0.88 per carry. Last year he drew 103 targets for 820 yards and posted the 10th-best EPA per target among backs. That is a three-down feature back, not a committee piece.

This season he is carrying an offense that is otherwise not functioning. Atlanta ranks 32nd in offensive EPA and 32nd in passing EPA, has started three different quarterbacks in three weeks, and passes 9.5 points less than the situation predicts, 30th in the league. Running is the only thing that works: the team's rush EPA ranks 5th, he has 66% of the carries and all five goal-line attempts, and he leads every qualifying back in scrimmage yards per game. The volume is the plan, not an accident of game script.

The headline efficiency needs an asterisk. His 0.98 rushing yards over expected per carry comes almost entirely from Week 3 in Green Bay, where he finished 77.5 yards over expected on 29 carries for 194 yards, even with eight-man boxes on 31% of his runs. He was below expected in each of the first two games, and his 15 runs up the middle average 2.93 yards with negative EPA. The ugly receiving EPA (-0.336 per target, 41st of 49) is mostly a Cooper Rush artifact: Rush threw him 14 of his 16 targets at -0.475 EPA each, 12 of the 16 came behind the line, and one incompletion over the middle cost nearly four points by itself. He has also fumbled twice and lost neither, which is luck, not a skill.

The outlook is better than the first two weeks suggested. Rush is inactive for the Saints game, the big runs have come when he gets outside, and New Orleans gives up explosive runs more than almost anyone and is missing its every-down linebacker. The volume is secure, the career trend says the elusiveness is real, and his receiving should drift back toward his norm once the quarterback stops checking down behind the line.

strengths.title: Locked-in volume in every situation
strengths.body: He has 66% of the team's carries, every goal-line carry, and the most scrimmage yards per game of any qualifying back. Atlanta's passing game ranks last and the staff runs well above expectation, so his role grows rather than shrinks with the quarterback chaos. Three straight seasons at a 68-78% snap share say this role is durable.

strengths.title: Creates yards beyond the blocking
strengths.body: His rushing over expected has climbed every year of his career, and the 2025 mark ranked 7th at the position, so this is a real skill, not a hot streak. Week 3 showed the ceiling: 194 yards against a defense loading the box on nearly a third of his runs. The season-to-date rate will cool, but the skill should keep him above expected over a full year.

strengths.title: Outside runs produce the big plays
strengths.body: Runs to either end have been his best plays: 11.75 yards a carry with a 50% explosive rate around right end, 13.6 around left end. These are 13 carries combined, so read it as a tendency rather than a fact. It still fits his profile as a back who wins in space, and it matters most against defenses that leak explosive runs.

concerns.title: Efficiency rests on one game
concerns.body: He was below expected as a runner against Pittsburgh and Carolina, and the whole season rate is carried by the Green Bay game against a defense now ranked 27th. Runs up the middle have been poor, at under 3 yards a carry with a 20% stuff rate. The career trend says he is better than the first two weeks, but 5.3 yards a carry is unlikely to hold.

concerns.title: Short yardage and third down stalls
concerns.body: On four short-yardage carries he lost yardage on average and was stuffed half the time, and his six third-down runs went for 1.17 yards a carry. Both samples are tiny. In an offense that can't threaten through the air, though, defenses can sell out on those downs, and that won't change until the passing game does.

concerns.title: Receiving value sunk by quarterback play
concerns.body: His per-target EPA ranks near the bottom, but almost all of it came from Cooper Rush's targets, three-quarters of them behind the line of scrimmage. He was a top-10 back by EPA per target in 2025, so this reflects his role in those games, not a flaw. The open question is volume: his targets fell from 10 to 4 to 2 across the three games.

trend.note: PPR output has gone 31.3, 11.1, 35.3, driven by game script: a 10-target game as a checkdown outlet, a 51%-snap day in a 3-34 blowout loss, then a 29-carry run game in a win. His rushing efficiency only turned positive in Week 3.

nextGame.headline: Soft, short-handed Saints run defense meets a run-first plan
nextGame.body:
New Orleans is one of the friendliest matchups a back can draw. The Saints rank 25th in rush EPA allowed and 31st in defensive success rate. They allow explosive runs at the fourth-highest rate in the league, and running backs average 152 yards and 1.33 touchdowns a game against them, both near the bottom. That fits what has worked for him, getting to the edge for chunk gains, and Atlanta will lean on the run regardless after passing well below expectation all year. Atlanta is a 1.5-point road underdog in a dome with 11 days of rest, and a game that close should keep the run plan intact for four quarters.

Availability cuts both ways. The Saints are without linebacker Kaden Elliss, a 100%-snap starter, along with edge Carl Granderson and reserve linebacker Anfernee Jennings, which thins the second level that has to fit his outside runs. On Atlanta's side, left tackle Jake Matthews has played every snap but is questionable with a groin injury, and the latest report has him ruled out mid-game against the Saints. That matters because his runs off left tackle have not been stuffed once in 15 tries. Cooper Rush is inactive as the emergency quarterback, so the checkdown-heavy target pattern from Week 1 is unlikely to repeat. Expect more of a Week 3-style workload than a 10-target day.

keyMatchups.title: Edge runs versus explosive-prone defense
keyMatchups.body: His best runs have come around the ends, and New Orleans allows explosive runs at one of the highest rates in the league. With Elliss out, the pursuit linebackers who chase those runs are thinner. This is the matchup most likely to produce a long run.

keyMatchups.title: Left tackle availability
keyMatchups.body: Matthews has played every offensive snap, and runs behind him have been steady, with no stuffs. If he can't finish, a backup left tackle would make the left side less reliable and push more runs to the right and the edges.

keyMatchups.title: Goal-line work against a generous defense
keyMatchups.body: He has taken every Atlanta goal-line carry and scored on two of five. New Orleans allows among the most running-back touchdowns per game, so any trip inside the 5 is likely his.

nextGame.watch: Whether Atlanta keeps feeding him outside zone to the edges once the Saints' depleted linebackers have to defend the perimeter, and who is playing left tackle.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume is the safest thing here: a team this run-dependent, with a bottom-ranked passing game, will keep giving him around two-thirds of the carries and all of the goal-line work. His yards over expected have risen four years running, so above-average efficiency is likely to hold, but 5.3 yards a carry will probably settle closer to his 2025 level of about 5 as the Green Bay game gets diluted. Touchdowns depend on how often the league's worst offense reaches the red zone, which caps them more than his role does.

The receiving side is where the upside is. Fourteen of his 16 targets came from a quarterback who is now inactive, and his career says he is a 90-100-target back who adds value as a receiver. If the quarterback spot settles, his target volume and EPA should both move back toward his norm, making him a more stable producer than his 11-to-35-point swings suggest.
swingFactors: Who settles in at quarterback and how often he targets the back
Jake Matthews' groin and the health of the left side of the line
Atlanta's red-zone trips in a last-ranked offense

bets.reason: He owns 100% of Atlanta's goal-line carries and has scored on two of five, and New Orleans allows 1.33 running-back touchdowns a game, 28th in the league. A thinned Saints front seven adds to it.

The Saints allow 152 yards a game to backs (31st) and rank 29th in explosive-run rate, without their 100%-snap linebacker. Matthews' uncertain status and a season average inflated by one 194-yard game keep this a lean rather than a like.

Thirteen of his catches came mostly from Cooper Rush, who is inactive. His targets fell from 10 to 4 to 2, and Penix threw to him only twice in Week 3, though that is a tiny sample against a strong receiving career.

The total is higher than any Atlanta game this year (two of three went under). Atlanta's offense ranks last in EPA and runs well above expectation, which shortens the game. The Saints are without Etienne and possibly Kamara against the league's top-ranked run defense.

confidence.note: Three games and three different starting quarterbacks, but a stable three-year workhorse baseline.
